key_terms.meaning: An append-only ledger of blocks, replicated across many nodes, where each block is linked to the previous one by its cryptographic hash.
The pseudonymous author of the 2008 Bitcoin design paper and the original Bitcoin software; identity unknown.
The first block of a chain; it has no previous block, so its previous-hash field is set to zero.
Spending the same digital coin twice; blockchain prevents it by ordering transactions and having nodes reject conflicts.
Code stored on the chain that runs automatically when its conditions are met, without a middleman.
One logical database spread over several machines, with read/write control held by an administrator.
A replicated, append-only record whose updates are validated by shared rules rather than by one administrator.
The problem of reaching agreement when some participants may send conflicting or false messages.
A system where one authority holds the data and decides every update.
Moving control of a system from one authority to many independent participants.
A chain anyone may read, submit transactions to and join as a validator, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum.
A chain where one organisation controls who may read, write and validate.
A chain governed by a fixed group of organisations that share validation rights, such as a group of banks.
The set of nodes allowed to propose and confirm blocks under the chain's consensus rules.
The metadata part of a block: previous hash, Merkle root, timestamp, difficulty target and a nonce.
A hash of the previous block stored inside the current block, which makes history tamper-evident.
The single hash at the top of a binary tree of transaction hashes; it summarises every transaction in the block.
The number of blocks between a block and the genesis block; genesis has height 0.
A computer running blockchain software that stores blocks, checks rules and relays data to peers.
A network where machines connect directly to each other and exchange data without a central server.

takeaways: Blockchain grew from digital-cash experiments into a general shared-ledger design after Bitcoin's 2008 release.
A distributed ledger differs from a distributed database because no single administrator decides which update wins.
Decentralization is a design choice with degrees; blockchain is one route to it, not the only one.
Every blockchain feature, such as immutability or transparency, is conditional and carries a cost in speed, storage or privacy.
Public, private and consortium chains are classified by who may read, write and validate.
A block is a header plus a body of transactions, and the previous-block hash links it to all earlier history.
Nodes differ by role: some only relay, some keep full history, some propose blocks.
Consensus rules, not trust in a company, decide which block becomes part of the chain.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to define blockchain, trace its evolution, compare it with a distributed database, and justify a chain type for a given business case.

bank.q: Define blockchain and explain how the technology moved through Blockchain 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0.
outline: Definition: append-only, replicated, hash-linked ledger
1.0: currency and payments, Bitcoin 2008
2.0: smart contracts and tokens, Ethereum
3.0: wider use such as supply chain, identity, land records
Each stage adds capability but keeps the same hash-linked data structure

bank.q: Distinguish between a distributed database and a distributed ledger, and explain why the ledger needs shared validation.
outline: Distributed database: one logical store, many machines, admin controls writes
Distributed ledger: replicated, append-only, updates accepted only if they satisfy shared rules
Conflict handling: database uses locking and admin decisions, ledger uses consensus
Byzantine Generals Problem as the reason agreement is hard
Example: two banks updating a shared balance without a clearing house

bank.q: List the main features of a blockchain and state one limitation or cost of each.
outline: Immutability: costly to reverse, so errors stay
Transparency: conflicts with privacy
Decentralization: slower and harder to govern
Auditability: storage grows forever
Disintermediation: legal responsibility still needed
Answer should pair every benefit with a cost

bank.q: Compare public, private and consortium blockchains on read, write and validate permissions, with one use case each.
outline: Public: open read, open write, open validator set, example Bitcoin
Private: restricted read and write, one organisation controls validators
Consortium: restricted read or write, validator set shared by known organisations
Table of who reads, who writes, who validates
Use cases: public for payments, private for internal records, consortium for inter-bank settlement

bank.q: Draw the structure of a block and explain each field of the header and the body.
outline: Header: previous block hash, Merkle root, timestamp, difficulty target, nonce, version
Body: list of transactions, usually with a transaction counter
Hash pointer links to previous block; changing history breaks all later hashes
Merkle root summarises transactions and allows short proofs
Block height and genesis block defined

bank.q: Five partner banks want one shared record of inter-bank settlements, with each bank validating updates but customer data hidden from outsiders. Recommend a chain type and justify the choice.
outline: Identify permissioned consortium chain
Read access restricted, write allowed to member banks, validator set fixed by governance
Why not public: privacy, throughput, regulatory accountability
Why not private: no single bank should control the ledger
Governance rules for adding or removing members

bank.q: A block contains four transactions with hashes T1 to T4. Describe step by step how the Merkle root is built and why it is useful.
outline: Hash each transaction to get leaf nodes
Pair T1,T2 and hash; pair T3,T4 and hash
Hash the two results to get the root
If the count is odd, the last hash is paired with itself
Use: one field in the header commits to all transactions
Use: Merkle proofs let a light client check one transaction

bank.q: Trace the life cycle of a transaction from a wallet to final inclusion in a block, naming the node roles involved.
outline: Wallet signs the transaction with the private key
Transaction broadcast to peer nodes
Nodes check signature, balance and format, then relay
Nodes hold it in a mempool
A block proposer picks transactions into a candidate block
Consensus accepts the block; other nodes validate and append it
Confirmations increase as later blocks are added

bank.q: A state government wants land records on a blockchain. Describe how decentralization would be applied and which parts should stay centralized.
outline: Define decentralization: control spread across participants
Route 1: distribute the ledger across revenue offices and banks
Route 2: allow citizens to verify their own record with a proof
Keep identity verification and legal title centralized by law
Consensus rules and validator set defined by statute
Discuss disputes: chain records the entry, courts decide ownership

bank.q: 'Blockchain removes the need for trust.' Examine this claim using the ideas of decentralization and blockchain myths.
outline: Blockchain replaces trust in one party with trust in rules, code and incentives
Trust shifts to: correct code, majority of validators, key custody
Myths: immutability is absolute, on-chain data is true, anonymity is guaranteed
Counter-examples: oracle data, exchange hacks, governance forks
Conclusion: trust is redistributed, not removed

bank.q: Explain double spending and the 51% attack, and evaluate why waiting for confirmations matters.
outline: Double spend: same coins sent to two receivers
Nodes order transactions; only the first valid one in the accepted chain counts
51% attacker: majority of hashing power can reorder or reverse recent blocks
Depth of a block: rewriting k blocks requires redoing their work
Practical rule: more confirmations for larger value
Trade-off: waiting time versus security

bank.q: For a supply-chain traceability project, compare a distributed database with a permissioned blockchain and recommend one.
outline: Criteria: who owns data, how many parties, trust level, throughput, privacy
Distributed database: fast, admin controlled, needs a trusted operator
Permissioned blockchain: shared validation, tamper-evident audit trail, slower
Volume and latency of supply-chain events
Recommendation with conditions, e.g. blockchain only if parties do not trust one operator

bank.q: Evaluate the scaling and governance trade-offs between public and consortium blockchains as transaction volume grows.
outline: Public chain limits: block size, block interval, global propagation
Scaling responses: larger blocks, layer-2 channels, sharding
Consortium: fewer validators, faster finality, but weaker censorship resistance
Governance: open improvement proposals versus a signed member agreement
Trade-offs: throughput versus openness, privacy versus verifiability

bank.q: Explain how nodes in a peer-to-peer blockchain network reach agreement when some nodes are faulty, and relate this to the Byzantine Generals Problem.
outline: Peer-to-peer topology: no central server, gossip relay
Fault tolerance: honest majority assumption
Byzantine fault: node may lie, not just crash
Consensus rules and block choice under competing proposals
Why permissioned chains handle faults differently from public chains

glossary.def: A chain of blocks, each holding transactions and the hash of the block before it, copied across many nodes.
A container of transactions plus a header, added to the chain after consensus.
The summary fields of a block: previous hash, Merkle root, timestamp, target and nonce.
The list of transactions carried inside a block.
The first block of a chain, with no predecessor and height 0.
The position of a block counted from the genesis block, which is height 0.
A cryptographic hash of the previous block stored in the current block, which makes tampering detectable.
A binary tree of hashes over transactions, whose top hash is the Merkle root.
The single hash that commits to every transaction in a block.
A block a node has assembled but not yet accepted by the network.
A computer running blockchain software that stores, checks and relays blocks and transactions.
A node that downloads and validates every block and keeps the complete ledger.
A network of machines that connect directly and exchange data without a server in the middle.
The process by which nodes agree on the next valid block and on the order of transactions.
Program code stored on the chain that executes automatically when its conditions are satisfied.
A ledger replicated across many nodes and updated under shared validation rules.
A database spread across machines but controlled by an administrator.
A failure where a node sends wrong or contradictory information instead of simply stopping.
Sending the same digital asset to two recipients; blocked by ordering and validation.
Distribution of control among many participants rather than one authority.
Open to anyone to join, read and validate without prior approval.
Restricted so that only approved participants may read, write or validate.
A group of organisations that jointly govern a shared permissioned ledger.
A split in the chain when two blocks at the same height are both accepted temporarily, or a permanent rule change.
